title: 626: Great Leaders Are Willing to Disappoint the Wrong Customers
author: Business Leader Daily
summary: This Business Leader Daily essay argues that the most consequential leadership decision in competitive positioning is not what you offer but what you are willing to withhold — and from whom. Organizations trying to be all things to all people end up memorable to no one. The author uses classical positioning theory (Ries, Collins, Dunford, Porter, Godin) to argue that every feature chase, segment expansion, or competitor-matching move feels reasonable in isolation but erodes competitive identity over time. The strategic implication is that every investment dollar should either deepen the value customers already come to you for or be resisted. When choices compound and reinforce each other over years — Collins's flywheel — a coherent position becomes a moat that competitors cannot easily replicate. The article closes with a simple reframe of the growth question: not 'How do we reach more people?' but 'What are we willing to give up to mean something specific to the people we most want to keep?'
points: A business's most important single decision — its positioning — happens in the room of the customer's mind without the business present. When nothing about your offering helps that choice, you do not lose dramatically; you fade into irrelevance.

Every add-on, feature match, or segment chase erodes the edges that once made an organization worth choosing. The cumulative effect of individually reasonable decisions can be a position so diluted it cannot defend against competition or command premium pricing.

The essence of positioning is sacrifice (after Al Ries): to own a place in the customer's mind, you must be willing to disappoint the wrong customers, turn away the wrong segments, and pass on opportunities that do not deepen what you already stand for.

When strategic investments compound behind a single coherent position — the flywheel effect — each investment builds on prior ones and creates cumulative difficulty for competitors to replicate. A competitor can match one feature; matching years of compounding coherence is a different problem.

The leadership reframe: stop asking 'How do we reach more people?' and ask 'What are we willing to give up to mean something specific to the people we most want to keep?' Deciding that question and funding it consistently is the foundation of long-game leadership.
quotes: Your business lives or dies on one decision your customers make without you in the room. They choose you, or they choose someone else. When nothing about your offering helps that choice in your favor, you do not lose in a single dramatic moment. You fade. You become irrelevant.

A new segment opens, so you chase it. A competitor adds a feature, so you match it. A loud prospect wants something outside your lane, so you build it. Each move feels reasonable on its own. Strung together over a few years, they sand down every edge that once made you worth choosing.
To own a place in the customer's mind, you have to be willing to give something up. The leaders who cannot bring themselves to disappoint anyone end up memorable to no one.

Your job as a leader is to make sure every dollar you invest deepens the value customers already come to you for, rather than scattering it across things they will never notice. When those investments line up behind a single position, they stop adding and start multiplying.

Get this right, and your focus hardens into something rivals struggle to copy. A clear position points every decision in the same direction, and that consistency is exactly what makes it hard to imitate.
The leaders who win the long game are rarely the ones who please everyone. They are the ones who chose.
